description: We are Astro Geeks — a team of five space and coding enthusiasts driven by curiosity, creativity, and a love for exploration. We enjoy learning new things, solving challenges, experimenting with technology, and pushing ourselves to discover something new every day. For us, there is always more to learn, more to build, and more to explore.
summary:
What if we could hear what our planet is trying to tell us?

Every day, Earth tells a story through shifting ocean currents, changing temperatures, lightning storms, and melting ice. Yet these powerful stories are often hidden within complex scientific visualizations, making them difficult to understand and less accessible to people who experience the world differently.

Our team developed Sonara, an interactive platform that transforms NASA Earth science data into meaningful soundscapes, allowing users to explore our changing planet through both sight and sound.

By connecting scientific patterns with music and interactive visualizations, we turn complex environmental information into an engaging, multisensory experience. Users can explore changes over time, discover patterns, and experience Earth science beyond traditional charts and images.

Our mission goes beyond making data audible. We want to make science more inclusive, spark curiosity, and create a deeper connection between people and the planet we all call home.

Because understanding Earth shouldn't depend on sight alone.
details:
Sonara - Project Details

Giving Earth a Voice

Earth has always been telling us its story. We just needed to find another way to listen.

Every second, our planet generates extraordinary amounts of scientific information. Oceans move, temperatures change, and lightning illuminates the atmosphere. NASA captures these processes through powerful Earth observation systems, but much of their data remains difficult for the public to interpret, especially when presented exclusively through charts, numbers, and visualizations.

Our team created Sonara, an interactive Earth observatory that brings scientific data, sound, and immersive design together.

Sonara reimagines how people experience Earth science. Instead of asking visitors to interpret complex datasets on their own, we transform real observations into interactive visualizations and musical interpretations, making environmental information more engaging, approachable, and accessible.

An Experience Designed to Inspire Curiosity

We wanted Sonara to feel like entering an observatory, not opening a spreadsheet.

The experience begins with a cinematic introduction that welcomes visitors into a carefully designed digital environment. At its center is an interactive, three-dimensional Earth, built with detailed planetary textures, atmospheric effects, clouds, lighting, and smooth camera movement.

Visitors can explore the globe before entering Mission Control, the central navigation interface that connects our scientific experiences.

Each stage was designed with a consistent visual identity, purposeful animations, intuitive navigation, and responsive layouts.

Our team also developed English and Arabic interfaces, including right-to-left layout support, allowing a wider audience to explore the platform comfortably.

The experience includes additional accessibility features such as keyboard navigation, geographic coordinate selection, high-contrast controls, an optional spoken navigation guide, and text-based scientific explanations.

Our design philosophy is simple: scientific discovery should feel inviting, not intimidating.

Figure 1. Sonara's immersive 3D observatory introduces visitors to an interactive journey through Earth science.

Turning Earth's Data into Sound

At the core of Sonara is data sonification: translating scientific measurements into meaningful audio.

Our team developed a processing and playback workflow that connects NASA observations to musical characteristics such as pitch, rhythm, intensity, and duration.

Using scientific datasets, our software extracts relevant measurements, validates them, and prepares them for interactive exploration.

The resulting experiences synchronize sound with visual information, giving users two complementary ways to understand the same environmental phenomenon.

Our platform currently brings together three major scientific experiences.

1. The Living Ocean — Listening to the Currents

Oceans are constantly moving, transporting heat and influencing the global climate. Yet understanding their movement through traditional velocity maps can be challenging.

Using NASA's OSCAR (Ocean Surface Current Analysis Real-time) dataset, we developed a visual and auditory representation of large-scale ocean surface circulation.

Animated particles move according to the dataset's estimated eastward and northward surface-current velocity components, creating flowing patterns that illustrate ocean circulation across the globe.

Visitors can navigate through twelve months of 2023 observations, examine specific geographic locations, and explore current speed and direction through interactive scientific readouts.

We also developed multiple data-derived musical interpretations, including our original Deep Ocean soundtrack and a complementary Bassoon layer that highlights selected current conditions.

An additional spatio-temporal comparison module, developed from NASA OSCAR observations and being integrated into the team platform, enables users to compare monthly ocean-current measurements across locations and time.

This work combines scientific data processing, mathematical interpolation, synchronized audiovisual playback, and interactive geographic exploration.

Rather than simply showing an animation, we built an experience where the movement of water becomes something users can both see and hear.

2. The Electric Sky — Discovering the Rhythm of Lightning

Lightning is one of Earth's most energetic and visually dramatic natural phenomena.

Using historical observations from NASA's International Space Station Lightning Imaging Sensor (ISS LIS), Sonara transforms satellite-observed lightning activity into a geographic musical representation.

The experience uses geographic and temporal information from lightning observations to generate musical patterns, allowing users to explore how recorded lightning activity varies across locations and observation periods.

An animated scanner travels across a world map while generated notes reflect the underlying observations. Visitors can explore historical observation dates, inspect geographic areas, and view scientific information alongside the synchronized audio.

A frequency visualization and playback controls help connect what users hear to the data-driven process producing the sound.

The result is an alternative way to experience the distribution and intensity of observed lightning activity.

3. Global Temperature — Hearing the Patterns of Change

Global temperature change is often presented through colored maps or numerical statistics. Sonara introduces an additional sensory dimension.

Using NASA's GISTEMP temperature anomaly data, we developed an interactive global temperature experience.

A color-coded visualization represents temperature anomalies relative to NASA's 1951–1980 reference period.

As a scanning line moves across the map, spatial temperature-anomaly patterns influence the generated musical notes. Users can navigate between months, explore geographic regions, and examine how the scientific measurements are translated into sound.

The visualizations and sound are linked through defined mathematical mappings, preserving a traceable connection to the underlying scientific information.

This allows visitors to experience patterns of warming and cooling through an audiovisual interpretation rather than relying exclusively on visual comparisons.

Interactive Exploration Beyond Playback

Sonara was designed to encourage active exploration rather than passive observation.

Across the scientific experiences, our team developed a shared interface that brings together:

  • Interactive geographic maps with zooming, panning, and location selection.
  • Scientific information panels displaying observed measurements and relevant units.
  • Date and month navigation for exploring historical records.
  • Synchronized audio playback, interactive waveforms, and playback controls.
  • Geographic and temporal exploration modes.
  • Full-map measurements and location-specific scientific readings.
  • Clear explanations of data sources, limitations, and sonification methods.

A particularly important feature is data-driven temporal synthesis, which allows visitors to listen to changing measurements across available observation dates, either for a broader geographic view or a selected location.

This makes Sonara more than a collection of prerecorded soundtracks: it becomes an interactive environment in which users can choose what to investigate.

Technology, Engineering, and Integration

Building Sonara required combining several disciplines into one coherent platform.

We developed the web application using React, TypeScript, JavaScript, HTML, CSS, Vite, Three.js, and React Three Fiber.

Three.js supports our interactive 3D Earth, while browser graphics technologies provide scientific maps, animated visualizations, and interactive data displays.

For audio, we used the Web Audio API alongside original, data-derived recordings, developing separate systems for synthesized sound, synchronization, playback controls, and waveform visualization.

Scientific data preparation involved Python, NumPy, xarray, netCDF4, and JSON, allowing us to process and validate Earth observation data before connecting it to the interface.

We used Git and GitHub for collaborative development, version control, and integration of the team's work.

One of our major engineering challenges was bringing independently developed scientific modules into a shared interface while preserving their individual data mappings and functionality.

We worked to maintain consistent navigation, synchronized playback behavior, accessible controls, responsive layouts, and transparent scientific information across the platform.

The development process also included automated tests for scientific-data consistency, navigation, interaction, audio behavior, and browser presentation.

Creativity Guided by Scientific Integrity

What makes Sonara different is the relationship between its scientific foundation and its artistic presentation.

We did not want to create music that merely accompanies beautiful images of Earth. We wanted the information itself to influence the listening experience.

That required making careful choices about how environmental measurements become musical parameters while avoiding misleading scientific interpretations.

We also distinguish between actual NASA observations and the visual or musical transformations created from them.

Our soundscapes are artistic interpretations of scientific observations and derived datasets, not literal recordings of ocean currents, lightning, or global temperature. The audio is generated through mathematical and creative mappings that translate environmental information into musical characteristics.

This distinction is essential to our approach: creativity should make science more understandable without changing what the science actually says.

Our Intended Impact

Sonara is designed for students, educators, science enthusiasts, and curious people who want to engage with Earth science in a more intuitive way.

By combining visual, auditory, and interactive approaches, we aim to broaden participation in scientific exploration and provide alternatives to experiences that rely entirely on visual interpretation.

We believe that environmental understanding begins with curiosity, and curiosity grows when people can connect with information in personally meaningful ways.

Our longer-term vision is to extend this approach to additional interconnected Earth systems, including polar ice, changing seas, and other environmental processes.

Sonara does not simply transform data into sound. It transforms scientific exploration into an experience.

We built it because our planet has extraordinary stories to tell, and we believe more people deserve the opportunity to hear them.
